entries.title: The project builds with Rust 1.100.0
entries.summary: The Docker build stage moves from rust:1.99-slim-trixie to rust:1.100-slim-trixie, and a new rust-toolchain.toml pins channel = "1.100.0" with the rustfmt and clippy components.
highlights: The project builds with Rust 1.100.0. The Docker build stage moves from rust:1.99-slim-trixie to rust:1.100-slim-trixie, and a new rust-toolchain.toml pins channel = "1.100.0" with the rustfmt and clippy components. Cargo resolves that file before the rustup default, so a local build, the workflows and the release pipeline all compile with the same compiler instead of following whatever stable the machine carries.

Every GitHub workflow installs Rust 1.100.0 explicitly (dtolnay/rust-toolchain@1.100.0) instead of the moving stable ref. The build-local-artifacts job of the release workflow now pins the toolchain before dist build, so the binaries published in a GitHub Release are compiled with 1.100.0 rather than the stable the runner happened to ship. The pin is a hand-written addition, kept out of dist init's reach by the existing allow-dirty = ["ci"] in dist-workspace.toml.

Nothing else changed. The full gate is green on 1.100.0 without touching a single source file: cargo fmt -- --check, cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings, 1 824 unit tests, the duplication gate (0.9% exact, 1.6% near) and all 23 E2E suites.
No re-index needed. Cargo.lock only records the new package version.

entries.title: The packaged Cargo.lock no longer references a yanked crate
entries.summary: It recorded chacha20 0.10.1, which is yanked on crates.io, so cargo publish warned about it and the published .crate carried that lock.
highlights: The packaged Cargo.lock no longer references a yanked crate. It recorded chacha20 0.10.1, which is yanked on crates.io, so cargo publish warned about it and the published .crate carried that lock. It is now 0.10.2. Only cargo install knot-server --locked was affected, and only by the warning: chacha20 is reached through rand 0.10, which the lock records but no enabled feature uses, so no compiled code changes.

entries.title: Upgrade knot to 1.16.2
entries.summary: That release only moves knot's build toolchain to Rust 1.100.0: no API, behaviour or index format changed, so no re-index is needed.
highlights: Upgrade knot to 1.16.2. That release only moves knot's build toolchain to Rust 1.100.0: no API, behaviour or index format changed, so no re-index is needed.

Build with Rust 1.100.0. The Docker build stage installs the 1.100.0 toolchain instead of 1.98.0. A new rust-toolchain.toml pins the channel (with rustfmt and clippy), and every GitHub workflow installs dtolnay/rust-toolchain@1.100.0 instead of the moving stable ref. The release workflow also pins the toolchain in build-local-artifacts before dist build, so the artifacts attached to a GitHub Release are compiled with 1.100.0 rather than whichever stable the runner carries.

entries.title: explore_file no longer returns a partial structuredContent (knot-server#12)
entries.summary: It held only markup_count and markup_references (plus ambiguous_path_candidates when present), while the outline was only in the text.
highlights: explore_file no longer returns a partial structuredContent (knot-server#12). It held only markup_count and markup_references (plus ambiguous_path_candidates when present), while the outline was only in the text. MCP clients that read structuredContent when it is present lost the whole file outline. The tool now returns text only, like the other six tools; the text already carries the markup summary and the ambiguous path candidates.

The serverInfo description and the explore_file, find_callers and search_hybrid_context descriptions list every indexed language family instead of only Java/TypeScript (or Java, Kotlin, C# and TypeScript).
No re-index needed.

entries.title: ort-load-dynamic cargo feature (#54)
entries.summary: The default build links the prebuilt static ONNX Runtime that ort downloads, which needs glibc 2.38+ / libstdc++ 13+ to link and a CPU with AVX to run (Illegal instruction otherwise).
highlights: ort-load-dynamic cargo feature (#54). The default build links the prebuilt static ONNX Runtime that ort downloads, which needs glibc 2.38+ / libstdc++ 13+ to link and a CPU with AVX to run (Illegal instruction otherwise). With --features ort-load-dynamic, nothing is downloaded or linked, and the binaries load Microsoft's official shared library at run time from ORT_DYLIB_PATH. It must be ONNX Runtime 1.27 or newer; 1.28.0 is the version ort targets. The binaries built this way need glibc 2.34 and no libstdc++. Library consumers (knot-lite, knot-server) forward it with ort-load-dynamic = ["knot/ort-load-dynamic"]. The default build is unchanged.

With that feature, Embedder::init loads ONNX Runtime before any model download. A missing or too old library becomes an error naming ORT_DYLIB_PATH and the minimum version, instead of a panic in the first embedding call. pipeline::embed::runtime::ensure_loaded() is public so consumers can check earlier, and it is a no-op in the default build. The first outcome is cached for the process, because ort 2.0.0-rc.13 cannot safely retry a failed load.

make build / make install and the CI binaries for E2E build with default features instead of --all-features, which would now turn on ort-load-dynamic and require the shared library at run time. Clippy and unit tests keep --all-features.
Unit tests (feature ort-load-dynamic, so they run under --all-features) cover the library path resolution, the error message, the cached failure, and Embedder init failing before any download.

entries.title: ort-load-dynamic cargo feature
entries.summary: It forwards knot's feature of the same name: knot-server loads Microsoft's official ONNX Runtime shared library (1.27 or newer) from ORT_DYLIB_PATH instead of linking the prebuilt static one, which…
highlights: ort-load-dynamic cargo feature (knot 1.16.0, knot#54). It forwards knot's feature of the same name: knot-server loads Microsoft's official ONNX Runtime shared library (1.27 or newer) from ORT_DYLIB_PATH instead of linking the prebuilt static one, which needs a CPU with AVX and glibc 2.38. A missing or too old library stops the server at startup with an error naming ORT_DYLIB_PATH. The "Running on CPUs without AVX2" recipe now uses cargo build --release --features ort-load-dynamic instead of editing Cargo.toml with cargo add ort.
Upgrade knot to 1.16.0. Default builds are unchanged. No re-index needed.
make build / make install use default features. --all-features would now turn on ort-load-dynamic, and the binary would then need the shared library at run time.

entries.title: Incremental re-indexing no longer leaves duplicate entities
entries.summary: On every sync or webhook run, the previous entities of a modified file were never deleted, because the deletion compared absolute paths with the repo-relative paths stored in Neo4j and Qdrant.
highlights: Incremental re-indexing no longer leaves duplicate entities (knot 1.15.1, knot#53). On every sync or webhook run, the previous entities of a modified file were never deleted, because the deletion compared absolute paths with the repo-relative paths stored in Neo4j and Qdrant. Every entity that moved to another line or was removed from the file stayed next to its new copy, so find_callers resolved several targets, listed callers twice and showed members that no longer exist. Edges from unchanged files and other repositories into a re-indexed file are now re-pointed at its new entities.

Existing indexes keep their duplicates until a full re-index. Delete its .knot/index_state.json in the workspace and trigger a sync, or run knot-indexer --clean on it with the server's database settings.

entries.title: Incremental runs no longer leave stale duplicates of the entities of modified…
entries.summary: The previous entities of a modified file were never deleted: the deletion compared the discovered paths (under the repository root) with the repo-relative file_path stored since v1.5.1, so nothing…
highlights: Incremental runs no longer leave stale duplicates of the entities of modified files (#53). The previous entities of a modified file were never deleted: the deletion compared the discovered paths (under the repository root) with the repo-relative file_path stored since v1.5.1, so nothing matched. Entities whose UUID did not change were overwritten, but every entity that moved to another line or was removed from the file survived next to its new copy, with its edges, in Neo4j and Qdrant. find_callers then resolved several targets and listed each caller twice, and explore_file and search showed members that no longer exist. Measured on a live knot-server index of 15 repositories, by comparing duplicates before and after one --clean re-index: about 6 100 stale entities in 10 of them (2 584 in browser-control-mcp, 2 212 in knot, 569 in knot-server).

Edges from unchanged files into a modified file survive its re-indexing. Since its entities are now deleted and re-created, the edges from files that are not re-parsed (and from other repositories) are captured before the deletion and re-pointed at the re-indexed entity with the same file, FQN, kind and signature, the nearest by line when several match. Edges into entities that no longer exist are dropped.

New suite run_incremental_e2e.sh (fixture testing_files/incremental/): a repository is indexed, then changed and re-indexed incrementally. A method moved down, a method removed and a file deleted must leave one copy of each entity in explore, callers (CLI and MCP) and search. The edge from an unchanged caller must follow the moved method, and the edge into the removed one must disappear. Unit tests cover the repo-relative deletion keys and the edge restoration grouping and query.
Run knot-indexer --clean once on repositories indexed incrementally since v1.5.1 to drop the duplicates already stored. Later incremental runs keep the index clean.

entries.title: Compact find_callers answers (#52)
entries.summary: The Markdown answer of the MCP tool and of knot callers --output markdown keeps every count but lists only what an agent needs.
highlights: Compact find_callers answers (#52). The Markdown answer of the MCP tool and of knot callers --output markdown keeps every count but lists only what an agent needs. References made from test code (test files, Rust #[cfg(test)]) are counted and not listed: each group ends with +N in tests, and the Found line states how many there are. A single-repository answer names its repository once, on the Found line, as (repo: name), while a multi-repository answer still labels every row. Rows are one line each, with the signature on that line when it is not empty, and a file's <module> row (its import) is folded into the file's other rows. Row shape is unchanged (- \name\ (kind) at \path:line\``) and so is the JSON output, which lists every row.
include_tests parameter on find_callers (CLI --include-tests) lists the references made from test code.

Reference rows now carry is_test_context, so the search summaries of #50 count Rust #[cfg(test)] callers as test code. The reference queries did not return the flag before, so those callers were reported as production callers. JSON rows gain the is_test_context field.

Token-efficiency benchmark re-run on today's snapshots (spring-ai b6b5767, puppeteer 08e7b1a, knot 421b515): 87.4% fewer tokens (≈7.9×) across the nine tasks, against 76.1% with v1.14.1 and 73.5% with v1.12.4 on the same snapshots. The callers rows went from 29 772 to 4 372 tokens. Listing test references too brings the total to 80.4%. The raw measurements now record the knot version and the snapshot commits.
